artiest/johnny-dyani.text:
Johnny Mbizo Dyani (1945 to 1986) was a South African jazz bassist, singer and pianist. He grew up in Duncan Village near East London, in the Eastern Cape. In the early 1960s he played in the Blue Notes, South Africa's first mixed jazz band, alongside trumpeter Mongezi Feza, alto saxophonist Dudu Pukwana, tenor saxophonist Nikele Moyake, pianist Chris McGregor and drummer Louis Moholo. In 1964 the group fled South Africa in order to play freely, far from an apartheid system that did not allow Black and white musicians to perform together.

In 1966 Dyani toured Argentina with Steve Lacy's quartet, where The Forest and the Zoo was recorded. In 1971 he founded his own group, Earthquake Power, and a year later, with Feza and the Turkish percussionist Okay Temiz, the group Xaba. He lived in Copenhagen and later in Sweden, where he recorded many albums under his own name. He also played with Dollar Brand, Don Cherry, Steve Lacy, David Murray, Joseph Jarman, Han Bennink, Mal Waldron and Pierre Dørge. In 1986 he died suddenly after a performance in West Berlin.

After his death the surviving Blue Notes made the album Blue Notes for Johnny. Pierre Dørge named a record Johnny Lives, and David Murray wrote the piece Mbizo. In a tribute, Pallo Jordan wrote that his music above all sounded of joy in life. Dyani shows how South African jazz in exile changed Europe.
artiest/johnny-dyani.listen: Listen to Song for Biko and notice the bass as the leading voice, and how African singing and free jazz come together.

artiest/johnny-gentle.text:
Johnny Gentle was the stage name of John Askew (1936 to 2024), a singer and songwriter from Liverpool. He trained as a carpenter, built his own guitar from a borrowed book and sang Everly Brothers songs in clubs. After a job on a luxury ocean liner, he entered talent contests under various names. In London he won a competition at the Locarno Ballroom in Streatham. In 1959 the manager Larry Parnes had him sign a contract with Philips Records and gave him his name.

The singles Wendy and Milk from the Coconut were released in 1959 but did not reach the charts. An EP, The Gentle Touch, missed them as well. His place in history stems from a short tour in May 1960. Parnes held auditions in Liverpool for groups to back his artists, and chose the Silver Beetles to accompany Gentle in Scotland. They played from 20 to 28 May 1960 in towns such as Alloa, Inverness and Peterhead. The group consisted of John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, Stuart Sutcliffe and drummer Tommy Moore.

On the posters they appeared only as Johnny Gentle and his group. They played songs such as Raining in My Heart and C'mon Everybody. On the tour Gentle wrote the song I've Just Fallen For Someone, by his own account with Lennon's help. Adam Faith later recorded it. Gentle said he rated the group highly, and later also that he had suggested to Parnes that he sign them. In this way he is a footnote in the earliest history of The Beatles.
artiest/johnny-gentle.listen: Listen to Wendy and notice how a British crooner from 1959 sounds, before the Beatles changed the sound of British pop.

artiest/johnny-green.text:
Johnny Green (1908 to 1989), whose full name was John Waldo Green, was an American composer, arranger, conductor and pianist from New York. He was taught by Herman Wasserman, among others, and went to Harvard at fifteen. Between semesters the bandleader Guy Lombardo heard his orchestra and had him write dance arrangements. His first hit, Coquette in 1928, was written for Lombardo. His father wanted him to become a stockbroker, but Green left Wall Street for music.

His most famous song is one of his earliest: Body and Soul, written in 1930 for Gertrude Lawrence and later a jazz standard. He also wrote Out of Nowhere, Bing Crosby's first number one, I Cover the Waterfront and I Wanna Be Loved. From 1930 to 1933 he was an arranger and conductor at Paramount Pictures. He then led his own orchestra and, until 1940, conducted the orchestras for Jack Benny's shows. At Paul Whiteman's request he wrote larger works, such as Night Club, which Whiteman performed at Carnegie Hall in 1933.

Later he wrote and conducted film music. He won four Oscars for his film scores and a fifth as producer of a short musical film. In 1972 he was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame, and he has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Jazz musicians recorded his songs, and film music of his, such as Raintree County, is still being reissued.
artiest/johnny-green.listen: Listen to Body and Soul, in every version you know, and notice how the melody deals with the chord changes. You will hear why jazz musicians keep returning to it.

artiest/johnny-griffin.text:
Johnny Griffin (1928 to 2008) was an American tenor saxophonist, nicknamed The Little Giant for his small stature and powerful playing. He learned music at DuSable High School in Chicago under Walter Dyett, starting on clarinet and moving via oboe to alto saxophone. At fifteen he was already playing with T-Bone Walker. Three days after graduating he joined Lionel Hampton's big band, and Hampton encouraged him to play tenor. In 1945, at seventeen, he was first heard on record.

After two years in the army he made his name in Chicago. Blue Note signed him before Riverside could, and in 1956 his first album, Introducing Johnny Griffin, was released, with Wynton Kelly, Curly Russell and Max Roach. A Blowin' Session from 1957 featured John Coltrane and Hank Mobley as guests. In 1957 he played for a few months with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers and then in Thelonious Monk's quartet, succeeding Coltrane. He can be heard on Thelonious in Action and Misterioso. In 1963 he moved to France and in 1978 to the Netherlands. There he played in the big band of Kenny Clarke and Francy Boland, among others, and alongside the tenor saxophonist Eddie Lockjaw Davis.

Griffin is regarded as a pioneer of hard bop. His style rested on dizzying technique and an enormous stock of bebop phrases. He liked to quote from classical music and opera. He recorded extensively as a bandleader and kept playing until the month of his death. In 1995 he received an honorary doctorate from the Berklee College of Music.
artiest/johnny-griffin.listen: Listen to Introducing Johnny Griffin from 1956 and notice his speed: how long he can sustain a line full of notes without losing his powerful tone.

artiest/johnny-hodges.text:
Johnny Hodges was an American alto saxophonist, born in 1907 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and raised in Boston. His first instruments were drums and piano, which he largely taught himself. As a teenager he switched to the soprano saxophone. At fourteen he played for Sidney Bechet, who was impressed and gave him lessons. In 1924 he left for New York, where he played with Chick Webb, among others.

In 1928 Hodges joined Duke Ellington's orchestra, where he stayed, with a short interruption, until his death. He led the saxophone section there and became one of the orchestra's most recognisable voices. Ellington wrote pieces especially for him, such as Jeep's Blues and Confab with Rab, named after his nicknames Jeep and Rabbit. His saxophone is also central in Prelude to a Kiss, I Got It Bad (and That Ain't Good) and Passion Flower. From 1951 to 1955 he had a band of his own, in which John Coltrane played, among others. He then returned to Ellington.

Hodges had a pure, warm tone and played sparingly, in both the blues and ballads. He used a broad vibrato and glided smoothly from one note to the next. Benny Goodman called him the greatest alto saxophonist he had ever heard, and Coltrane saw him as his first model. He died in 1970. Ellington said afterwards that his orchestra would never sound the same again.
artiest/johnny-hodges.listen: Listen to Isfahan (1967) by Duke Ellington and His Famous Orchestra. Notice how Hodges makes his melody sing, with long notes and soft, gliding transitions between the pitches.

artiest/johnny-hoes.text:
Johnny Hoes (1917 to 2011) was a Dutch singer, producer, composer and lyricist. He was born in Rotterdam and grew up in Katendrecht, the son of a Dutch seaman and a Belgian mother. He played covers with The Four Dutch Serenaders. During the war years he lived in Limburg, where after the liberation he performed for American soldiers. In the late 1940s he was a supporting act for Bobbejaan Schoepen. From 1952 to 1963 he worked at Phonogram. From 1964 he made records for his own label, Telstar, with a studio of his own in Weert.

His own record Och, was ik maar bij moeder thuis gebleven is on record as the best-selling Dutch-language single ever. Other hits were De smokkelaar, Dat is het einde and Friet met mayonaise from 1974. He released records as a soloist, sometimes as Andy Field, and with others, including Johnny & Caesarine and Johnny Hoes & Ria Roda. Artists released on his label included De Alpenzusjes, the Zangeres Zonder Naam, Eddy Wally, Normaal, Doe Maar and Henk Wijngaard. He was also the producer of the worldwide hit De vogeltjesdans. On the radio he had a programme on the KRO and on television a show of his own on the VARA, Met een lach en een traan.

Hoes was called the king of the smartlap (the Dutch tearjerker), the man behind thousands of singalongs, carnival songs and songs about life. His albums cover the whole of Dutch popular life, from Kussen van Hawaii to Hup Ajax! and songs for Feijenoord. He remained active to a great age and in 2011 still recorded a final record, a duet with Stef Ekkel.
artiest/johnny-hoes.listen: Listen to Och, was ik maar bij moeder thuis gebleven and notice the simple melody and the emphasis on a text that everyone sings along to at once.

artiest/johnny-jordaan.text:
Johnny Jordaan was the pseudonym of Johannes Hendricus van Musscher, a Dutch singer of the levenslied, the Dutch variant of the French chanson. He was born in 1924, the son of a roofer, near the Westertoren, on the edge of the Jordaan, at that time a poor working-class district. He was already singing in the street at eight, together with his cousin Carel Verbrugge, later known as Willy Alberti. At fourteen he took the name Johnny Jordaan. After the war he got a regular job as a singer in the café De Kuil.

In 1955 he won the Jordaanfestival, a singing contest organised by the record company Bovema to find the best voices of the Jordaan. His first single contained two songs by Louis Noiret, De Parel van de Jordaan and Bij ons in de Jordaan. After being broadcast by the AVRO, it was an immediate hit. His best-known song, Geef mij maar Amsterdam, is felt by many Amsterdammers to be their own song. In a few months he sold hundreds of thousands of records and performed with Tante Leen at the Concertgebouw.

His style is recognisable by its hiccuping vibrato, called Mokum by the Amsterdammers. He became the uncrowned king of the Jordaan song and made the dialect of the Jordaan popular nationwide. The whole district, which had been poor since the nineteenth century, became fashionable. Jordaan died in 1989. He belongs in Dutch music history as the interpreter of a city's identity.
artiest/johnny-jordaan.listen: Listen to Geef mij maar Amsterdam and notice the singing: can you hear the hiccuping vibrato, and how the chorus is meant to be sung along to?

artiest/johnny-kidd-en-the-pirates.text:
Johnny Kidd & the Pirates were an English rock band built around the singer and songwriter Johnny Kidd. They signed to His Master's Voice in 1959 under the producer Walter J. Ridley. Their first single, the raw Please Don't Touch, which Kidd wrote himself, reached number 25 in the British charts in 1959. Their stage show was theatrical, in the vein of contemporaries such as Screaming Lord Sutch & the Savages.

Their most famous song is Shakin' All Over, which topped the British chart in 1960. It is known above all for its opening guitars and Joe Moretti's solo. The group played as a kind of early power trio, which impressed The Who, who put the song on Live at Leeds in 1970. The Canadian band The Guess Who took it to number one in Canada in 1965. After that the line-up changed, and when a new line-up arrived with Mick Green on guitar, the sound of A Shot Of Rhythm And Blues emerged, in which Green alternated lead and rhythm. That 1962 record is seen in retrospect as a link between British rock 'n' roll and British beat. Kidd later performed in a nineteenth-century costume with a large pirate ship as backdrop, and brandished a cutlass.

The group broke up when Kidd was killed in a car accident in 1966. Former members later performed as The Pirates, until the end of the 2000s. According to the CD sleeve of Live at Leeds, Shakin' All Over is the best British rock record from before The Beatles.
artiest/johnny-kidd-en-the-pirates.listen: Listen to Shakin' All Over and notice the opening: the guitar sets up the tense, menacing theme before the rest of the band joins in.

artiest/johnny-mercer.text:
Johnny Mercer (1909 to 1976) was an American lyricist, songwriter and singer, and co-founder of Capitol Records together with Buddy DeSylva and Glenn Wallichs. He was born in Savannah, Georgia. His mother sang sentimental ballads, his father old Scottish songs, and as a child he listened to fishermen and street vendors who spoke and sang in Gullah. The services in Black churches also drew him in. He had no musical training, could not read a score and used a notation system of his own, but at six he sang in a choir. At eleven or twelve he knew almost every song he had heard and wanted to know who had written them.

Mercer wrote the lyrics for more than twelve hundred songs, for films, Broadway shows and well-known standards. They include Autumn Leaves, Days of Wine and Roses, Hooray for Hollywood, I'm an Old Cowhand, for which he also wrote the music, and Moon River. He received eighteen Oscar nominations and won the Oscar for Best Song four times. He sometimes composed as well, even though he did not play the piano. As a singer he recorded his own and other people's songs from the mid-1930s to the mid-1970s, for example on Songs by Johnny Mercer in 1944.

His place in pop history is that of Tin Pan Alley's master of words, the man who gave other people's melodies lyrics that stuck. With Capitol Records he also founded a record label that became of great significance to the American music industry.
artiest/johnny-mercer.listen: Listen to Moon River and notice how the lyric, with short, simple words, evokes a feeling of wistfulness and longing.

artiest/johnny-otis.text:
Johnny Otis was an American bandleader, drummer, singer, producer and talent scout. He was born in 1921 as Ioannis Veliotes in Vallejo, California, to Greek immigrants. He grew up in a predominantly Black neighbourhood in Berkeley and chose at an early age to live as a member of the Black community. As a teenager he bought a drum kit and played in local bands and later in swing orchestras.

In 1945 Otis started his own band, which had a hit with Harlem Nocturne. In 1947 he opened the Barrelhouse Club in Watts, Los Angeles, with Bardu Ali. There he made his band smaller and hired singers, among them the teenage singer Little Esther, whom he discovered at a talent contest. With his California Rhythm and Blues Caravan he scored a string of R&B hits around 1950, such as Double Crossing Blues. In 1952 he produced the first recording of Hound Dog by Big Mama Thornton in Houston, on which he also played drums. He discovered Etta James, Jackie Wilson and Hank Ballard, and in 1958 he had a big hit of his own with Willie and the Hand Jive.

Otis is sometimes called the godfather of rhythm and blues. He gave countless young singers their first break and helped build the bridge from swing to R&B and rock 'n' roll. He was also a radio DJ, writer and preacher, and spoke out openly against racism. He died in 2012.
artiest/johnny-otis.listen: Listen to Willie and the Hand Jive (1958). Notice the rhythm that keeps coming back, a pattern also known as the Bo Diddley beat, and how the whole song is driven by it.

artiest/johnny-pacheco.text:
Johnny Pacheco (1935 to 2021), whose full name was Juan Pablo Pacheco Knipping, was a Dominican musician, arranger, composer, bandleader and producer. He was born in Santiago de los Caballeros. His father led, and played clarinet in, the orchestra Santa Cecilia, one of the most important Dominican big bands of the 1930s. When he was eleven the family moved to New York. He learned accordion, violin, flute, saxophone and clarinet, studied electrical engineering at Brooklyn Technical High School and later percussion at Juilliard.

In the 1950s he played percussion for Tito Puente and Xavier Cugat, among others. In 1954 he founded the Chuchulecos Boys with Eddie Palmieri and others. In 1959 he formed the charanga La Duboney with the pianist Charlie Palmieri, in which he played flute. He found Palmieri's style too refined and less marketable, and he opted for simpler arrangements based on son. He became a leading figure of the pachanga, a mixture of Cuban rhythms and Dominican merengue. Albums such as Mi nuevo tumbao... Cañonazo from 1964 and Pacheco te invitar a bailar from 1965 let you hear that period.

Pacheco founded Fania Records and was its musical director. He popularised the term salsa and set up the Fania All-Stars, a supergroup that showcased the best artists of the genre and brought him worldwide fame. In doing so he played a major role in the development of Latin American music. He was nominated for a Grammy nine times and in 2005 received the Latin Grammy for his lifetime achievement.
artiest/johnny-pacheco.listen: Listen to a Pacheco track from the 1960s, such as Mi nuevo tumbao, and notice the flute and the percussion, which together set down a danceable rhythm.

artiest/johnny-ramone.text:
Johnny Ramone's real name was John William Cummings, and he was born in 1948 in Queens, New York. He grew up in Forest Hills, was a greaser as a teenager and played in a band with the future Ramones drummer Tommy. Before success he worked as a plumber with his father. In the early 1970s he met Douglas Colvin, who would later become Dee Dee Ramone, while delivering dry-cleaning. They turned out to be devoted to both The Stooges and MC5. In January 1974 Johnny bought a second-hand blue Mosrite for just over fifty-four dollars, because it was the cheapest guitar in the shop.

With the singer Joey, Dee Dee and later the drummer Tommy, he formed the Ramones. They all took the surname Ramone. The first gig was on 30 March 1974. The debut album Ramones received good reviews but was not a commercial success: it got no higher than number 111 on the American album chart. Johnny and Joey were the only original members who stayed until the end in 1996 and they appeared on every album. In 2002 the band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Johnny played almost exclusively rhythm guitar and used almost nothing but downstrokes, with full barre chords and the occasional power chord. Together with his amplifier tone, this gave a more aggressive and rhythmic sound than that of his contemporaries and strongly influenced the early punk bands. In 2009 Time put him on a list of the ten best electric guitarists. He also appeared in almost a dozen films and wrote the autobiography Commando, which was published in 2012. He died in 2004.
artiest/johnny-ramone.listen: Listen to a track from the first album, Ramones, and notice the guitar: every stroke comes down, with no solo and no embellishment, and the rest of the group follows that tempo.

artiest/johnny-rotten.text:
Johnny Rotten's real name is John Lydon, and he was born on 31 January 1956 in London, in the poor district of Holloway. His parents were Irish working-class migrants. As the eldest of four brothers he often had to look after the others, because his mother was ill. At seven he survived a severe case of meningitis, in which he lost part of his memory.

In 1975 the manager Malcolm McLaren brought him into the Sex Pistols. Lydon stood out for his outspoken character, rebellious look and clothes. At his audition he sang along to I'm Eighteen by Alice Cooper. The guitarist Steve Jones gave him the nickname Johnny Rotten, because of his bad teeth. With the Sex Pistols he co-wrote Anarchy in the U.K., God Save the Queen and Holidays in the Sun. The group shocked the British media, and Rotten became the face of emerging punk. His sneering way of singing became the band's trademark. In early 1978 he quit during an American tour, and the group fell apart.

Afterwards he called himself John Lydon again and founded Public Image Ltd. That band was far more experimental and is sometimes called the first post-rock group. PiL made eight studio albums, with singles such as Public Image, Death Disco and Rise. Later Lydon presented television programmes and wrote two autobiographies. Despite their short existence, the Sex Pistols are regarded as one of the most influential groups in pop history.
artiest/johnny-rotten.listen: Listen to God Save the Queen by the Sex Pistols (1977). Notice how Johnny Rotten spits the words rather than sings them, with an exaggerated sneer in his voice, over a wall of simple, hard guitar chords.

artiest/johnny-st-cyr.text:
Johnny St. Cyr (1890 to 1966) was an American jazz banjoist and guitarist from New Orleans. His father died when he was eleven. His mother would not let him play her guitar, so he built one himself from a cigar box, fishing line and wire. When he could play chords as well as she could, she gave him her guitar. At fourteen he played in The Consumers Band, named after the beer that the friends of his brother brought along every Sunday. The band drew the biggest crowds at the Saturday fish fries.

In 1905 he left school and became an apprentice to a plasterer. He played with the National band and later came into the shop of the barbers and violinists Piron and Paul Dominguez, who had a lot of sheet music. He became one of the pioneers of jazz and played in the groups of Louis Armstrong, King Oliver, Jelly Roll Morton, Johnny Dodds and Kid Ory. He can be heard on the recordings of Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven. He himself wrote, among other pieces, Messin' Around, Buddy's Habit, High Fever and Oriental Strut.

St. Cyr played a Martin guitar, a four-string tenor banjo or a six-string banjo-guitar, which he made himself by attaching the neck of a guitar to a banjo. That gave a louder instrument with a jazz sound. He used a hard, thick plectrum, made from toothbrush handles, for a supple rhythm and clear single-note lines. He established the idea of the banjo in jazz, a combination that changed the banjo world. He saw himself as a working man, who liked playing without putting himself first.
artiest/johnny-st-cyr.listen: Listen to a recording by Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and notice the rhythm that the banjo keeps going behind it: tight, clear and always in the background.

artiest/johnny-ventura.text:
Johnny Ventura, nicknamed El Caballo Mayor, was a Dominican singer and bandleader of merengue and salsa. He was born in 1940 as Juan de Dios Ventura Soriano. At sixteen he won an amateur singing contest on the radio, and then many more, until he received a scholarship from the broadcaster La Voz Dominicana, with which he studied music, vocal technique and expression. In 1959 he took the name Johnny Ventura and sang in orchestras that played at dances. He worked with Luis Pérez's Combo Caribe and recorded his first LP with them. In 1963 he joined La Super Orquesta San José, as a singer and güira player.

In 1964, at the urging of a Cuban impresario, he started his own orchestra, Combo Show, which took an important place in popular Dominican music. In 1965 the albums La Coquetona, La Resbalosa and El Turun Tun Tun were released with that orchestra. In 1967 he travelled to the United States, where he became a star at once. The album Ah...! Yo no sé... No from 1971 became his first gold record. Songs such as Salsa pa' tu lechón, El Tabaco and Llegaron los caballos made him popular throughout the Caribbean.

Ventura helped modernise merengue, with faster rhythms, choreographed performances and influences from salsa and other Caribbean music. In 2004 he received a Latin Grammy for the album Sin Desperdicio and in 2006 the Latin Grammy for his lifetime achievement. He was also a politician: member of parliament from 1982 to 1986, deputy mayor of Santo Domingo from 1994 to 1998 and mayor from 1998 to 2002. He died in 2021.
artiest/johnny-ventura.listen: Listen to Salsa pa' tu lechón and notice the tempo and the brass, and how the singer encourages the dancers.

artiest/johnny-ventura-y-su-combo-show.text:
Johnny Ventura, born Juan de Dios Ventura Soriano and nicknamed El Caballo Mayor, was a Dominican singer and bandleader of merengue and salsa. He was born in 1940 and died in 2021. At sixteen he won a talent contest on radio and television, and received a scholarship from the broadcaster to study music, vocal technique and expression. In 1959 he took the name Johnny Ventura.

He sang in several bands, including the orchestra of Rondón Votau and, in 1961, that of the percussionist Donald Wild. In 1962 he sang with Luis Pérez's Combo Caribe, with whom he recorded his first twelve-track LP, including Cuidado Con el Cuabero. In 1963 the musical director Papa Molina brought him into La Super Orquesta San José. Later he led his own Combo Show, with which he recorded Patacón Pisao, a song from 1977.

Ventura received a Latin Grammy in 2004 for Sin Desperdicio, a Latin Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2006 and a place in the Latin Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2022. His political career is remarkable: he was a member of the House of Representatives from 1982 to 1986, deputy mayor of Santo Domingo from 1994 to 1998 and mayor from 1998 to 2002. Merengue is the national music of the Dominican Republic, with a fast rhythm of tambora, güira and accordion, and Ventura modernised it with a combo with brass and a show element that drew dancers.
artiest/johnny-ventura-y-su-combo-show.listen: Listen to Patacón Pisao and notice the breakneck rhythm of the drums and the güira, and how the brass and the singer alternate. Can you stand still?

artiest/jon-batiste.text:
Jon Batiste, born in 1986 in Metairie, Louisiana, grew up in Kenner and comes from the New Orleans musical Batiste family, which also includes Lionel Batiste of the Treme Brass Band and Milton Batiste of the Olympia Brass Band. At eight he played drums in the family band, the Batiste Brothers Band. At eleven, on his mother's advice, he switched to piano and had classical lessons for seven years. He also practised by transcribing songs from video games such as Street Fighter Alpha and Final Fantasy VII. His debut album Times in New Orleans was released when he was seventeen.

He studied jazz at the Juilliard School, where he earned his bachelor's degree in 2008 and his master's in 2011. Albums followed such as MY N.Y., Social Music and Hollywood Africans from 2018. From 2015 to 2022 he was, with his band Stay Human, bandleader and musical director of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. He collaborated with Alicia Keys, Stevie Wonder, Prince, Willie Nelson and Lauryn Hill, among others. In 2020 he wrote, with Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, the score for the Pixar film Soul, for which they received an Oscar, a Golden Globe, a Grammy and a BAFTA.

In 2021 he won a Grammy for Album of the Year with We Are. In total he won eight, from twenty-five nominations. The 2023 documentary American Symphony follows him as he composes his first symphony. He is also musical director of The Atlantic and creative director of the National Jazz Museum in Harlem. In this way he links the jazz tradition of New Orleans with today's pop culture and television.
artiest/jon-batiste.listen: Listen to a track from Hollywood Africans or from the album We Are and notice how jazz piano playing and elements from pop and gospel run together.

artiest/jon-christensen.text:
Jon Christensen (1943 to 2020) was a Norwegian jazz drummer. In the late 1960s he played with Jan Garbarek on several recordings of the composer George Russell, including The Essence of George Russell from 1967 and Electronic Sonata for Souls Loved by Nature from 1969. In 1967 he won prizes from the Norwegian jazz press and from the Norwegian Jazzforum, and in 1975 he was named Drummer of the Year by the European Jazz Federation. In 1977 he received the Spellemannprisen, the Norwegian music prize, and three more times with Masqualero.

Christensen is above all associated with the German label ECM. He played on many records there, with Keith Jarrett, Jan Garbarek, Terje Rypdal, Bobo Stenson, Eberhard Weber, Ralph Towner, Barre Phillips, Arild Andersen, Enrico Rava, John Abercrombie, Miroslav Vitous, Charles Lloyd and Tomasz Stanko, among others. He was a member of Keith Jarrett's European quartet of the 1970s, together with Garbarek and the bassist Palle Danielsson. That quartet recorded five albums for ECM, including Belonging from 1974 and My Song from 1977. Ralph Towner's Solstice from 1975 is also regarded as a milestone. With Arild Andersen he was a central figure in the group Masqualero, which reunited in 2003 for his sixtieth birthday.

Christensen made only one album under his own name, No Time for Time from 1976. His significance lies in his work as an accompanist: a drummer who leaves space, who adds colours and pulses instead of laying down a fixed rhythm. In this way he contributed to what is called the Nordic jazz sound, with an open, restrained atmosphere. He died in 2020.
artiest/jon-christensen.listen: Listen to Belonging by Keith Jarrett from 1974 and notice Christensen's playing on cymbals and drums: he accompanies without dominating and gives the lines of Jarrett and Garbarek room.

artiest/jon-lord.text:
Jon Lord was an English keyboardist and composer. He was born in 1941 in Leicester and had classical piano lessons from the age of five. Bach remained a fixed point of reference throughout his life, but as a teenager he also fell under the spell of American jazz and blues organists such as Jimmy Smith, who played a Hammond through a Leslie speaker. In London he played in clubs and sessions and in bands such as The Artwoods. In 1968 he founded Deep Purple together with Ritchie Blackmore, Ian Paice, Nick Simper and Rod Evans.

In the first years of Deep Purple, Lord found his own sound. He ignored synthesizers. He ran his Hammond organ through Marshall amplifiers, so that it sounded as loud and aggressive as Blackmore's guitar. This gave a heavy, distorted organ sound that provided the band with a rhythmic foundation. According to Ian Gillan, Lord also devised the organ motif of Child in Time. He also continued to bring rock and classical music together. The album Concerto for Group and Orchestra, for band and symphony orchestra, gave Deep Purple their first chart entry in Britain in early 1970. Later came works of his own such as Gemini Suite (1971), Sarabande (1976) and the Durham Concerto (2007).

Lord also played in Whitesnake and in Paice Ashton Lord. He stayed with Deep Purple until 2002, and between 1968 and 1976 he and Paice were the only permanent members. His hard organ playing was essential to the band's heavy sound and helped shape early heavy metal. He died in 2012. In 2016 he was inducted, with Deep Purple, into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/jon-lord.listen: Listen to Child in Time by Deep Purple. Notice the organ at the start and how, later in the song, it sounds just as loud and raw as Blackmore's guitar.

artiest/jonas-gwangwa.text:
Jonas Gwangwa (1937 to 2021) was a South African jazz musician, songwriter and producer, for more than forty years an important figure in South African jazz. He was born in Orlando East, part of Soweto, and became known as the trombonist of The Jazz Epistles. When that short-lived group broke up, he remained important, first in his own country and later abroad. In 1965 he took part in the concert Sound of Africa at Carnegie Hall, together with Miriam Makeba, Hugh Masekela and Letta Mbulu.

The apartheid government disliked him despite his fame, and in the 1970s he went into exile. He lived first in the United States, then for most of the 1980s in Gaborone in Botswana, where he founded the band Shakawe and joined the MEDU Art Ensemble of anti-apartheid musicians, visual artists and writers. After the South African army's attack on Gaborone in June 1985, in which twelve people were killed, he went abroad again. From 1980 to 1990, at the request of Oliver Tambo, he led Amandla, the cultural ensemble of the ANC, which told the story of the struggle against apartheid in music in more than forty countries.

Later he wrote film music, including for Cry Freedom from 1987. His song Cry Freedom was nominated for an Oscar and he played it at the ceremony in 1988. That year he also performed at the concert for Nelson Mandela's seventieth birthday at Wembley. In 1991 he returned to South Africa and in 1997 he wrote the theme for South Africa's bid for the Olympic Games. In 2010 he received the Order of Ikhamanga in gold.
artiest/jonas-gwangwa.listen: Listen to Cry Freedom from the 1987 film and notice how South African singing and an orchestral film sound together form a protest song.

artiest/jonathon-heyward.text:
Jonathon Heyward is an American conductor and cellist, born in 1992 in Charleston, South Carolina. He was not exposed to classical music at home. He first learned the cello and played chamber music. In 2009 he conducted for the first time, in the youth orchestra of the Mozart in the South Festival in Charleston. He studied conducting at the Boston Conservatory under Andrew Altenbach, worked there on operas by Puccini, Mozart and Britten, and completed his studies in 2016 at the Royal Academy of Music in London under Sian Edwards.

In 2015 he won the Besançon International Competition for Young Conductors. In 2016 he became assistant conductor of The Hallé and led the Hallé Youth Orchestra. In August 2021 he conducted at the Proms for the first time. From 2021 he was chief conductor of the Nordwestdeutsche Philharmonie, until the end of the 2023 to 2024 season. In 2022 it was announced that he would become the new music director of the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra, from the 2023 to 2024 season. He is the first conductor of colour in that position with the orchestra. His contract was extended in 2025 through the 2030 to 2031 season.

In 2023 he also became music director of the Lincoln Center Festival Orchestra, the orchestra that used to belong to the Mostly Mozart Festival. In 2025 he added the title of artistic director there. In October 2023 Time put him on its list of Next Generation Leaders. His album A New Dawn was released in 2022. He is thus one of the young conductors renewing orchestral life in the United States.
artiest/jonathon-heyward.listen: Listen to A New Dawn from 2022 and notice how the orchestra plays under his direction, with precise ensemble playing and great attention to the colours of the different instrumental groups.

artiest/joni-mitchell.text:
Joni Mitchell was born in 1943 as Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, in the Canadian province of Alberta. She is one of the most important singer-songwriters of the 1960s and 1970s: she wrote her own songs, sang them herself and told of her own life in them. The music guide AllMusic called her, in 2011, perhaps the most important female artist of the late twentieth century.

At nine she contracted polio, which weakened her left hand. She therefore devised other tunings for her guitar, which later became her trademark: when strummed open, the strings already form a chord. Her debut Song to a Seagull (1968) was produced by David Crosby. Clouds (1969) contains her own version of Both Sides Now, and Ladies of the Canyon (1970) Big Yellow Taxi and Woodstock. Blue (1971) is a sober, personal album that Rolling Stone placed at number 3 in its list of best albums in 2020. With Court and Spark (1974) she moved towards jazz. On Hejira (1976) the bassist Jaco Pastorius plays, and Mingus (1979) she made together with Charles Mingus, who died before the record was finished.

Mitchell showed that a woman in pop did not have to be only a singer, but also a writer, guitarist and arranger. Her songs were recorded by many others, such as Both Sides Now by Judy Collins and Big Yellow Taxi by Counting Crows (2002). After a ruptured brain aneurysm in 2015, she was back on a stage in 2022, at the Newport Folk Festival.
artiest/joni-mitchell.listen: Mitchell wrote Big Yellow Taxi (1970) about a car park in Hawaii where green mountains had once been visible. Listen to the guitar in an open tuning: the strings sound together as a chord, and the cheerful accompaniment is at odds with the angry lyric.

artiest/jonny-greenwood.text: Jonny Greenwood was born in 1971 in Oxford and is the guitarist and multi-instrumentalist of the band Radiohead. He briefly studied music but was mostly self-taught, with a great interest in Messiaen and Penderecki. His first film score was for the documentary Bodysong (2003). For Paul Thomas Anderson's There Will Be Blood (2007) he wrote string music with clusters and gliding tones, which makes the oil, the desert and the protagonist's obsession audible. With Anderson he also made The Master (2012) and Phantom Thread (2017). The latter, by contrast, sounds romantic, with piano and strings in the style of the 1950s. For Jane Campion's The Power of the Dog (2021) he had a cello plucked like a banjo.
artiest/jonny-greenwood.listen: Notice the strings sliding as a single mass of sound, with clusters and glissandi instead of a clear melody.

artiest/joost-klein.text:
Joost Klein is a Dutch musician, rapper, singer and former YouTuber, born in 1997 in Leeuwarden and raised in the Frisian village of Britsum. In 2010 he started his YouTube channel EenhoornJoost, with sketches and mini-documentaries. When he was thirteen his father died of cancer, and a year later his mother. His older brother and sister looked after him afterwards. In 2016 his debut EP Dakloos was released, after which he focused on music. He was briefly with TopNotch, then founded his own label, Albino Sports.

He released the mixtape Scandinavian Boy in 2017, in 2018 the album M van marketing together with the rapper Donnie, and also in 2018 the little poetry collection Albino, named after his 2019 album. His best-known songs are Wachtmuziek from 2022, Friesenjung from 2023 with Ski Aggu and Otto Waalkes, and Europapa from 2024. He has made ten studio albums, two of which reached the top ten of the Dutch Album Top 100. His music is mainly hip hop, with influences from drum and bass, hardstyle, hyperpop and gabber.

Europapa was chosen to represent the Netherlands at the 2024 Eurovision Song Contest and became his first number one in the Dutch Top 40 and the Single Top 100. He came second in his semi-final but was disqualified by the EBU shortly before the final over allegations of misconduct. The Swedish prosecution authority dropped the case in August 2024, because it could not prove any criminal conduct. He is still making music, became a coach on The Voice of Flanders and will go on his first international tour in 2026.
artiest/joost-klein.listen: Listen to Europapa and notice the contrast between the festive, hardstyle-like beat and the simple, almost childlike repetition in the lyrics.

artiest/jordi-savall.text:
Jordi Savall is a Spanish conductor, composer and viol player, born in 1941 in the Catalan town of Igualada. He started in the school choir at six, studied from 1959 to 1965 at the conservatoire of Barcelona and specialised in early music. From 1968 to 1970 he studied at the Schola Cantorum Basiliensis in Basel under August Wenzinger, whom he succeeded in 1974 as teacher of the viola da gamba. Since the 1970s he has been one of the great names in early music. He made the viol family known to a broad audience.

In 1974 he founded, with his wife, the soprano Montserrat Figueras, Lorenzo Alpert and Hopkinson Smith, the ensemble Hespèrion XX, since 2000 Hespèrion XXI. It played with great liveliness and at the same time maximum historical accuracy. In 1987 he founded La Capella Reial de Catalunya in Barcelona, a vocal ensemble for music from before the eighteenth century. In 1989 followed Le Concert des Nations, a Baroque orchestra that also plays Classical and Romantic repertoire. He made more than two hundred recordings, including of viol music from France, such as Pièces de viole du second Livre from 1975.

Savall plays music from the Middle Ages to the Romantic period and also records music from outside Europe. For Les Routes de l'Esclavage from 2017 he worked with African musicians of the ensemble 3MA. In the Orient-Occident projects he played, with musicians from the Middle East, Arabic, Christian and Sephardic music from medieval Al-Andalus, Syria, Morocco and Turkey. He also founded festivals, such as the Festival musique et histoire in Fontfroide and the Jordi Savall Festival in Catalan monasteries.
artiest/jordi-savall.listen: Listen to one of his recordings of French viol music, such as Pièces de viole du second Livre, and notice the warm, singing tone of the viol and how it differs from a cello.

artiest/jordi-savall-en-hesperion-xxi.text:
Jordi Savall is a Spanish conductor, composer and viol player, born in 1941 in Igualada. Since the 1970s he has been one of the great figures in Western early music. He made the viola da gamba family popular again in performances and recordings. He started in the school choir at six, studied at the conservatoire of Barcelona and then at the Schola Cantorum Basiliensis in Basel, where he became professor of viola da gamba in 1974.

In 1974 he founded, with his wife, the soprano Montserrat Figueras, Lorenzo Alpert and Hopkinson Smith, the ensemble Hespèrion XX, since 2000 Hespèrion XXI. His style combines great liveliness with as much historical accuracy as possible. In 1987 he founded La Capella Reial de Catalunya in Barcelona, a vocal ensemble for music from before the eighteenth century, and in 1989 the orchestra Le Concert des Nations, mainly for Baroque music. Later he also played with his children Arianna and Ferran.

Savall increasingly recorded music from other traditions. With musicians of the ensemble 3MA he made Les Routes de l'Esclavage (2017), with African folk music. In the Orient-Occident programmes he played, with Middle Eastern musicians, Arabic, Christian and Sephardic music from medieval Al-Andalus. In the same way he brings the Ottoman music of Cantemir, such as Der makâm-ı 'Uzzâl, to a large audience. His importance lies in the way he plays early music as a living tradition in dialogue with other cultures.
artiest/jordi-savall-en-hesperion-xxi.listen: Listen to Der makâm-ı 'Uzzâl usûleş Devr-i kebîr and notice the interplay of strings, flute and percussion: can you hear how a melody is richly ornamented and keeps returning in a fixed rhythmic cycle?

artiest/jorge-bolet.text:
Jorge Bolet (1914 to 1990) was a Cuban-American concert pianist, conductor and teacher. He was born in Havana and studied at the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia, where he also taught from 1939 to 1942. His teachers included Leopold Godowsky, Josef Hofmann and Moriz Rosenthal, a famous pupil of Franz Liszt. In 1937 he won the Naumburg competition and gave his first recital. During his service in the American army he ended up in Japan, where he conducted the Japanese première of The Mikado.

In 1960 he played the piano sounds for the film Song Without End, a biopic about Liszt with Dirk Bogarde, which won an Oscar for best music. Even so, for decades he remained criticised by American critics, who said he aimed too much at Romantic virtuosity, and his recordings from the 1960s were released on small labels. Only in 1974 did he break through nationally, with a grand recital at Carnegie Hall. From 1968 to 1977 he taught at Indiana University and afterwards briefly headed the piano department of the Curtis Institute, succeeding Rudolf Serkin. In 1978 he signed with Decca, at the age of sixty-four, and there followed recordings of a large part of his repertoire.

Bolet is remembered above all for his performances of great Romantic music, especially Liszt, César Franck and Chopin. In 1984 the channel A&E had him give masterclasses in Bolet Meets Rachmaninoff on Rachmaninoff's Third Piano Concerto, followed by a complete performance. He died in 1990 of heart failure.
artiest/jorge-bolet.listen: Listen to his recording of Liszt's Années de pèlerinage from the 1980s and notice the singing melody that keeps sounding above the fast, heavy chords of the left hand.

artiest/jorge-cafrune.text:
Jorge Cafrune (1937 to 1978) was one of the most popular Argentine folk singers of his time and also a tireless researcher and promoter of indigenous culture. He was born on the estancia La Matilde in the province of Jujuy, into a family of Syrian-Lebanese descent. He went to school in San Salvador de Jujuy and had guitar lessons from Nicolás Lamadrid. In 1957 he recorded his first album with the group Las voces de Huayra, which in 1960 became Los cantores del Alba, with Ariel Ramírez as manager.

From 1962 he performed at the folk festival of Cosquín. In 1966, on a journey through small villages, he met the young singer José Larralde. In 1967 he began the journey De a caballo por mi patria, as a tribute to the leader Chacho Peñaloza. Dressed as a traditional gaucho, he travelled through Argentina to spread his art and message. Albums such as Que seas vos from 1964 and Yo he visto cantar al viento from 1968 preserve his work.

After years in Spain he returned in 1977 to Argentina, which was then under Videla's military dictatorship. The government saw a threat in his outspoken music, especially in his controversial song Zamba de mi esperanza. He said that he would keep singing it if his people asked for it, even though it was not on the permitted list. On 1 February 1978 he was hit at night, on horseback on a main road, by a van and died within twelve hours. For Argentines he is a symbol of folk music and of resistance.
artiest/jorge-cafrune.listen: Listen to Zamba de mi esperanza and notice the zamba as a dance and song form: a calm, swaying rhythm with a guitar and a voice singing full of restrained feeling.

artiest/jorge-drexler.text:
Jorge Drexler is a Uruguayan musician, actor and doctor, born in 1964 in Montevideo. His father was a German Jew from Berlin who fled the Nazis at the age of four with his parents, via Bolivia to Uruguay. His mother was Catholic, of mixed Spanish, French and Portuguese descent. Drexler played piano from the age of five, later had guitar and composition lessons, and, like his parents, studied medicine, specialising in ear, nose and throat. During his studies he hitchhiked through Brazil.

In 1995 he performed in Montevideo as the support act for the Spanish singer Joaquín Sabina, who invited him to Madrid and introduced him to other Spanish musicians. In 1996 he recorded the album Vaivén in Spain. He then moved to Spain and made four more albums: Llueve, Frontera, Sea and Eco. His first album La luz que sabe robar was released in 1992 and Radar in 1994. In 2001 he wrote two songs with Rosario Flores for her album Muchas Flores.

His song Al otro lado del río was heard in the film The Motorcycle Diaries. In 2005 it won the Oscar for Best Song, making Drexler the first Uruguayan with an Oscar and the song the first Spanish-language song to receive the prize. On stage he was not allowed to sing it: Antonio Banderas and Carlos Santana did. In accepting the prize he recited two verses. After that came 12 segundos de oscuridad in 2006, including a cover of High and Dry by Radiohead. He lives in Spain for most of the year, but records his albums partly in Uruguay, with Uruguayan musicians.
artiest/jorge-drexler.listen: Listen to Al otro lado del río and notice the quiet guitar and the soft voice, and how the lyric describes a journey to the other side of a river.

artiest/jorge-rossy.text:
Jorge Rossy, also called Jordi, is a Spanish jazz drummer, pianist and vibraphonist, born in 1964 in Barcelona. His father and sister played piano at home. He began on drums at eleven and got a drum kit a year later. At fourteen he bought a cheap vibraphone, which he practised on for two years. He then took up the trumpet, to learn to listen better. Between 1980 and 1989 he toured extensively with Spanish jazz musicians and with international names such as Woody Shaw and Kenny Wheeler.

In 1989 he went to Boston to study trumpet at the Berklee College of Music, but within two years he chose drums. He played in Danilo Pérez's trio and for two years in Paquito D'Rivera's sextet. In 1991 he moved to New York and played on early recordings by contemporaries such as Mark Turner, Chris Cheek and Kurt Rosenwinkel. In 1995 he began touring and recording with the Brad Mehldau Trio. He also worked with Joshua Redman and with Charlie Haden, Carla Bley, Joe Lovano and Chick Corea.

In 2000 Rossy went back to Barcelona to bring up his family and to concentrate more on piano. In 2006 he recorded his first album as a leader, with Albert Sanz on Hammond organ. Later releases included Stay There, his first recording on vibraphone, and Beyond Sunday. His career shows how a European jazz musician made a place for himself in the New York scene of the 1990s and later returned to his own city.
artiest/jorge-rossy.listen: Listen to a recording by the Brad Mehldau Trio from the 1990s and notice the drums: Rossy plays lightly and sensitively, reacts to the piano and does not lay down a fixed pattern.

artiest/jose-alfredo-jimenez.text:
José Alfredo Jiménez (1926 to 1973) was a Mexican actor and singer-songwriter whose songs are regarded as the foundation of modern regional Mexican music and the ranchera. He was born in Dolores Hidalgo, in the state of Guanajuato. His father died when he was ten, and his mother moved with the family to Mexico City. He worked from a young age to contribute to the family income, including as a waiter in a restaurant. There he began writing and singing songs with a group, Los Rebeldes. As a boy he liked playing goalkeeper.

The singer Miguel Aceves Mejía says he discovered him. According to him, Jiménez played no instrument and did not even know the Spanish word for waltz. On Mejía's instructions he auditioned at the radio station XEW, together with the Mariachi Vargas and Rubén Fuentes. He sang a cappella, including Ella. Mejía then recorded Ella, Yo, Serenata huasteca and Tu recuerdo y yo. Jiménez went on to write more than a thousand songs, including Me equivoqué contigo, Paloma querida, Media vuelta, El Rey, El jinete, Amanecí en tus brazos, and Que te vaya bonito, and Camino de Guanajuato, in which he sings of his home state.

His songs are about love, loss, pride and drink, in simple language that everyone knows. One of his last television appearances, in 1973, was for his last song, Gracias, together with his wife, the singer Alicia Juárez. He died that same year at the age of forty-seven in Mexico City of complications from cirrhosis of the liver. His albums, such as Ella… la que se fue from 1958 and La enorme distancia from 1961, are still being reissued.
artiest/jose-alfredo-jimenez.listen: Listen to Que te vaya bonito and notice the mariachi accompaniment with trumpets and violins, and the plain, honest way in which the singer sings of a farewell.

artiest/jose-padilla.text:
José Padilla (1955 to 2020) was a Spanish DJ and producer of ambient music, best known as the DJ at the bar Café del Mar in Ibiza. He was born in Barcelona and moved to Ibiza in 1975. For years he sold mixtapes at the bar and there, in 1991, he got the resident DJ slot. By his own account he sold a hundred mixtapes a day and went from door to door in London looking for a record deal.

In 1994 he compiled the first Café del Mar album for the London label React. The series now runs to twenty-five volumes, with a number of related compilations, and led to the bar's own label. Padilla chose the tracks for the first six volumes and for the twentieth-anniversary release. His first album of his own, Souvenir, was released in 1998 on Mercury Records, with contributions from chill-out musicians such as Lenny Ibizarre and Paco Fernández. Navigator from 2001 received a Latin Grammy nomination for best instrumental album.

Later he was no longer a resident DJ at Café del Mar, but he performed worldwide. In 2007 the compilation series Bella Musica was released, separate from Café del Mar. In 2015 So Many Colours was released and in August of that year he played an Essential Mix on BBC Radio 1 for the first time in twenty years. His name is linked to a particular idea of relaxation: music for the sunset hour. He died in 2020 of bowel cancer.
artiest/jose-padilla.listen: Listen to a track from Souvenir from 1998 and notice the slow tempo, the soft synthesizers and the guitar, which together create a sunset atmosphere.

artiest/joseph-canteloube.text:
Joseph Canteloube (1879 to 1957) was a French composer, musicologist and writer, best known for his arrangements of folk songs from the Auvergne for voice and orchestra, the Chants d'Auvergne. He was born in Annonay in the Ardèche, into a family with roots in the Auvergne. From the age of six he had piano lessons from Amélie Doetzer, a friend of Chopin. In 1901 he began taking lessons by letter from Vincent d'Indy, and in 1907 he went to the Schola Cantorum in Paris, where he remained until the First World War.

He wrote, among other works, the suite Dans la montagne for piano and violin, Colloque sentimental for voice and string quartet, the orchestral piece Eglogue d'Automne and the song cycle L'Arada. His first opera, Le mas, won the Prix Heugel in 1925, but the management of the Opéra-Comique was far less enthusiastic than the jury, and the opera was not performed until 1929 and never again after that. His second opera, Vercingétorix, premièred at the Paris Opéra in 1933, but was criticised for containing too little theatre.

In 1925 he founded, with other natives of the Auvergne in Paris, the group La Bourrée, to make the folklore and beauty of their region known. Canteloube believed that peasant songs, in terms of feeling and expression, often reach the level of the purest art. He also published songs from other regions, such as Rouergue, Limousin and Quercy. His Chants d'Auvergne have been recorded many times, sometimes together with Villa-Lobos's Bachianas Brasileiras No. 5, as on releases from the 1960s and 1980s.
artiest/joseph-canteloube.listen: Listen to one of the Chants d'Auvergne, such as Baïlèro, and notice the singing melody that keeps rising above a soft, almost floating orchestra.

artiest/joseph-carl-breil.text: Joseph Carl Breil was born in 1870 in Pittsburgh and was a singer, conductor and composer before he went to work for the cinema. For the American screening of Queen Elizabeth (1912) he wrote one of the first original film scores in the United States. His best-known work is the music for D.W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation (1915). Breil combined themes of his own with familiar melodies from operas, folk songs and nineteenth-century popular music. A large orchestra played the score in the premiere theatres. The love theme 'The Perfect Song' became a hit. The film is notorious for its glorification of the Ku Klux Klan, and that racism also resonates in the way the music characterises groups.
artiest/joseph-carl-breil.listen: Hear how familiar quotations stand beside original themes and so give characters, groups and places a fixed sound.

artiest/joseph-haydn.text: Joseph Haydn was for almost thirty years Kapellmeister to the Esterházy princes, far from the big city, with an orchestra of his own to experiment with. In this way, as he himself said, he was forced to become original. He gave the symphony and the string quartet their classical form. In his Symphony No. 94 from 1791, written for London, a sudden loud chord in the calm second movement startles the listener awake.
artiest/joseph-haydn.listen: Listen to the opening of Die Schöpfung and hear how Haydn paints chaos with chords that nowhere come to rest.
